candidates.name: Dora
candidates.description: Dora (Dataflow-Oriented Robotic Architecture) is middleware for composing AI-based robotic applications as low-latency, distributed dataflow pipelines.

triage.rule: docs/CURATION.md inclusion gate; ADR 023 role test
triage.finding: Ships an installable CLI (cargo install dora-cli) and Python API (pip install dora-rs) with releases, CI, and a public node hub, so a maintained run path is documented. Its documented outcome is a declarative dataflow graph whose nodes mix software, models, and hardware: the node hub lists ready-made nodes for cameras, YOLO, LLMs, and TTS, and the README documents a ROS2 bridge so a graph can carry a model node's output straight to a robot's actuators. No existing role names composing a dataflow graph that spans model nodes and physical hardware nodes, and the property is stated directly in the README's feature list and node-hub description without reading the source tree.

candidates.name: OM1
candidates.description: OM1 is a modular AI hardware-abstraction layer that lets LLM-driven agents control heterogeneous robots over ROS2 and Zenoh.

triage.rule: docs/CURATION.md inclusion gate; ADR 023 role test
triage.finding: Ships pre-built binaries for four platforms plus a documented build-from-source path, with a five-minute quick start that gets a running instance talking. Its documented outcome is a runtime that takes camera, microphone, LIDAR, and web input, routes it through a configurable choice of LLM and VLM providers, and issues physical actions -- motion, autonomous navigation, and spoken conversation -- on humanoid and quadruped robots as well as simulators. No existing role names a runtime whose delegated outcomes include moving a physical body rather than only files, applications, or the web, and the property is stated directly in the README's opening description and quick-start walkthrough without reading the source tree.

candidates.name: openpi
candidates.description: openpi holds Physical Intelligence's open-source vision-language-action robot policy models (pi0, pi0-FAST, pi0.5) and the packages to run or fine-tune them.

triage.rule: docs/CURATION.md inclusion gate; ADR 023 role test
triage.finding: Publishes an installable Python package (uv/pip) plus three named vision-language-action checkpoint families (pi0, pi0-FAST, pi0.5), downloaded from a hosted bucket rather than bundled in the repository, with documented fine-tuning and serving code. The README's own remote-inference workflow runs the checkpoint on a separate server and streams its predicted action_chunk output to the robot over a websocket connection, and its quickstart shows inference producing that action_chunk from a camera image and a language instruction. No existing role names a package whose delegated outcome is streaming a trained policy's action output to a physical robot rather than to a software tool, and this is stated directly in the README's quickstart and remote-inference sections without reading the source tree.

candidates.name: Safari SDK
candidates.description: Safari SDK provides full lifecycle tooling for Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics models, including checkpoint access, serving, evaluation, and fine-tuning.

triage.rule: docs/CURATION.md inclusion gate; ADR 023 role test
triage.finding: Publishes a Python SDK (pip install safari-sdk) for accessing, serving, evaluating, and fine-tuning Gemini Robotics checkpoints; the README says most of that functionality requires joining a Trusted Tester program rather than downloading open weights. The README documents a bundled framework whose Embodiments component 'connect agents to physical robot systems' and whose worked example wires a conversational agent to control an Aloha robot, with a Tools component described as letting the agent perform robot control. No existing role names a developer package whose own documentation describes connecting a model-driven agent to physical robot hardware, and this is stated directly in the README's Agent, Embodiments, and Tools sections without reading the source tree.

candidates.name: Alpamayo
candidates.description: Alpamayo is NVIDIA's open reasoning vision-language-action model that pairs autonomous-vehicle driving trajectories with chain-of-causation reasoning.

triage.rule: docs/CURATION.md inclusion gate; ADR 025 Models collection boundary
triage.finding: Ships Apache-2.0 inference code plus a link to separately Hugging-Face-hosted weights under a distinct OpenMDW-1.1 licence, and its own disclaimer describes the release as provided solely for research, experimentation, and evaluation -- lacking real-world sensor access and required safety mechanisms, and explicitly 'not a fully fledged driving stack,' positioned as a building block rather than a deployed system. Its documented output is a predicted multi-second driving trajectory (waypoints) paired with a natural-language reasoning trace; the trajectory is numeric rather than text, image, audio, video, or PDF, and the reasoning trace is auxiliary to it rather than the release's primary output. No model type or modality already in this catalog's vocabulary names a released policy whose primary documented output is a predicted trajectory.

candidates.name: Spot
candidates.description: Spot is Boston Dynamics' commercially sold agile mobile robot for autonomous site inspection and remote operation.

triage.finding: Boston Dynamics publishes extensive Spot SDK developer documentation (dev.bostondynamics.com) covering the robot's API services, autonomy, and data systems, and that documentation site is itself the only stably citable first-party page found: every page on bostondynamics.com proper -- the product page, '/terms/', and '/spot-sales/' alike -- embeds a live WordPress cache-metrics comment whose hit/miss counters differ on every request, confirmed by fetching each of them twice in a row and finding the bytes differ both times, so none of them can be pinned for stable re-verification. Read live (not pinned), '/terms/' is a generic website Terms of Use governing use of bostondynamics.com itself -- content ownership, site access -- not a purchase agreement, EULA, or licence for the product, and '/spot-sales/' routes pricing and purchase through a 'Contact Sales' form rather than a published price or sale terms. No product-specific terms or licence establishing a reviewed source model and complete licence list are published on any first-party page; capability is shown in vendor-authored demonstrations and documentation, which are evidence of the claim rather than of a governing agreement.

candidates.name: Unitree G1
candidates.description: The Unitree G1 is a commercially sold humanoid robot with force-position hybrid control and imitation- and reinforcement-learned manipulation skills.

triage.finding: Unitree publishes a public price (from $13.5K) for the G1 on its own product page and a Terms & Policies page, but that page's only substantive content is an after-sales warranty policy for the physical hardware (repair eligibility, damage exclusions, shipping responsibility); it establishes no software licence, source-model classification, or complete licence list for the robot's onboard AI stack or control software. The site links an 'Official Open Source' page, but that page renders no first-party list of components or licences in its own markup. No authoritative first-party source establishes a reviewed source model and complete licence list for the product as sold.

candidates.name: Figure
candidates.description: Figure is an AI robotics company building a general-purpose humanoid robot for commercial deployment.

triage.finding: figure.ai is served through a Vercel CDN edge cache: repeated fetches within a single verification session return identical bytes with a constant ETag and a climbing 'age' header (observed on the terms-and-conditions, privacy-policy, accessibility-statement, and home pages alike), so the site reads as stable while any one review is underway. But a shared footer icon component embeds a randomly generated SVG gradient identifier that is baked in at origin render time; that value changes only when the edge cache invalidates and Vercel re-renders from origin on its own stale-while-revalidate cadence, not on every request. That makes a hash pinned to any figure.ai page unsafe to rely on indefinitely -- it can hold for an entire review session and still not survive to a later recheck once the cache regenerates, which is exactly the failure this review hit once already when a Wayback capture of this same page was hashed moments after being triggered and had not yet settled. The terms-and-conditions page was read live: it is a generic website Terms and Conditions, dated February 2023 in its own body text, governing use of figure.ai itself (account access, electronic communications, linked sites) with no mention of the robot as a product, its sale, its licensing, or its onboard software, and no product page publishes a price or purchase path. That reading is a first-party observation, not a durably re-verifiable citation, for the CDN-cache reason above; the site's own sitemap is cited instead because, as a static file with no templated component, it does not carry the same regeneration risk, and it establishes from a stable first-party source that the terms page exists and when Figure's content system last touched it. No product-specific terms or licence establishing a reviewed source model and complete licence list are published on any first-party page, and no page on the domain carrying that content can be durably pinned for a checkable citation in the first place.

evidence.label: Sitemap (the only figure.ai resource found to be byte-stable across repeated fetches; it confirms the terms-and-conditions URL exists but carries no terms content itself)

candidates.name: 1X NEO
candidates.description: NEO is 1X's humanoid home robot, sold to perform household chores and provide personalized in-home assistance.

triage.finding: 1X publishes public pricing and reservation plans for NEO on its own order page ($499/mo subscription or $20,000 ownership, a refundable $200 deposit), but the Terms and Conditions page linked from both the product and order pages returns HTTP 404 -- the document does not exist at review time, even though the sibling Privacy Policy page resolves. No reachable first-party page therefore establishes a reviewed source model or complete licence list covering the hardware, its built-in large language model, or its Redwood AI vision-language model; the order page's own feature list describes capability through marketing prose rather than a governing agreement.

candidates.name: LeRobot
candidates.description: LeRobot provides models, datasets, and tools in PyTorch for end-to-end robot learning, aiming to make real-world robotics more accessible.

triage.rule: docs/CURATION.md inclusion gate; ADR 023 role test
triage.finding: Ships an installable PyPI package (pip install lerobot) with a documented training and control run path and a hardware-agnostic Robot interface. Its documented outcome is taking a trained policy's output and sending it straight to physical hardware: the README's own code example reads 'action = model.select_action(obs)' followed by 'robot.send_action(action)', across supported arms, humanoids, and other devices, including vision-language-action policies. No existing role names a framework whose distinguishing behavior is sending a model's output to a physical actuator rather than to a software tool, and the property is shown directly in the README's code example without reading the source tree.

candidates.name: Isaac GR00T
candidates.description: Isaac GR00T N1.7 is NVIDIA's open foundation model for generalist humanoid robots.

triage.rule: docs/CURATION.md inclusion gate; ADR 025 Models collection boundary
triage.finding: Publishes pre-trained checkpoints under the NVIDIA Open Model License alongside Apache-2.0 code implementing a vision-language-action architecture whose action head is a diffusion transformer that denoises continuous actions. The README's own workflow overview ends with 'Connect Gr00tPolicy to your robot controller,' and its deployment section documents a server-client architecture where a policy server sends predicted actions to a client controlling real DROID hardware. No model type or modality already in this catalog's vocabulary names a released policy whose primary documented output is continuous robot-control actions rather than text, image, audio, video, or PDF, and this is stated directly in the README's workflow-overview and deployment sections without reading the source tree.

candidates.name: OpenVLA
candidates.description: OpenVLA is an open-source vision-language-action model for robotic manipulation.

triage.rule: docs/CURATION.md inclusion gate; ADR 025 Models collection boundary
triage.finding: Publishes pre-trained checkpoints on Hugging Face that, per the README's own licensing note, inherit the Llama-2 Community License even though the repository's code is MIT-licensed. The README states the released checkpoints are trained 'to generate actions, and actions alone,' and its getting-started example predicts an action from a camera image and instruction and passes the result straight to 'robot.act(action, ...)'; a separate deployment script serves the model over a REST API for integration into existing robot control stacks. No model type or modality already in this catalog's vocabulary names a released policy whose sole documented output is a robot action rather than text, image, audio, video, or PDF, and this is stated directly in the README's getting-started example without reading the source tree.
